name: inverted-index
title: inverted-index: build, persist and open a compact binary inverted index
interface:
Module `lib/index-format.mjs`.

```stub
export function buildIndex(docs: Array<{ id: string, title: string, body: string }>, meta: object): object;
export function writeIndex(dir: string, index: object): void;
export function openIndex(dir: string): object;
```

- `buildIndex(docs, meta)` tokenizes each document with text-analyzer's `tokenize`,
  counting title and body occurrences separately, and returns an in-memory index that
  carries `meta` through unchanged.
- `writeIndex(dir, index)` removes any previous index in `dir` (no stale file survives
  a rewrite), creates it, and serialises the index as a compact binary: a small JSON
  header holding counts, meta and section offsets, then variable-length-integer encoded
  document ids, document lengths, the sorted term dictionary and the postings.
  The whole index must stay well under the size of the corpus it was built from.
- `openIndex(dir)` returns a reader over the files on disk, decoding lazily; it throws
  an Error mentioning the directory when the index is missing, and an Error mentioning
  the format when the magic/version bytes are wrong. The reader exposes:
    reader.docCount   -> number of indexed documents
    reader.avgDocLen  -> mean weighted document length
    reader.meta       -> the object passed to buildIndex (docs, skipped, ...)
    reader.docId(i)   -> the id string of document i
    reader.docLen(i)  -> the weighted token length of document i
    reader.postings(term) -> Array<{ doc: number, body: number, title: number }>,
                             ascending by doc, empty for an unknown term.
nl_description: The storage half of the search engine: the on-disk shape of the index and the reader that queries go through. It owns the size dimension (index bytes relative to corpus bytes) and the cold-start half of the speed dimension — a query process must be able to open the index and pull one term's postings without parsing everything. Also owns the "fully overwritten per run" rule: re-indexing a different corpus must leave nothing of the old one behind.
